units: an experienced cook takes his apprentice to task over the state of his cutting tool
the blunted blade crushes the herbs instead of severing them
the crushed leaves give up their sap too early
the colour of the preparation turns dull as a result
the scent of the preparation is weakened by it
the apprentice claims he sharpened the tool the day before
the fault comes from an angle poorly held during sharpening
the superior asks for the operation to be done again in front of him
text: The head cook took his apprentice aside and spoke plainly about the state of the chopping blade. Blunt as it had become, it crushed the herbs rather than severing them, and crushed leaves give up their sap far too early. Colour drains out of the preparation, he said, and the scent thins away to almost nothing. The apprentice protested that he had put the tool to the stone only the day before. His superior held the edge up against the window light and showed him where the metal had gone round. The angle had wandered while the blade travelled over the stone, so the cutting line was lost without anyone noticing. Proof of it sat on the plate: a sauce gone brown where a bright tone had been expected. Care over the upkeep decides the flavour at the end, he concluded, and he asked the young man to sharpen the blade again in front of him.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: meat from animals killed before the cold season spoiled very quickly
the lack of artificial cold left rural households exposed to shortage
salt supplied the first remedy to this problem
a heavily concentrated salt solution draws the water out of the tissues
this drying out stops micro-organisms from multiplying
aromatics were later added to the preserving bath
preserving thus became a way of seasoning as well
smoking added a protective layer at the surface
these methods passed from one person to the next through direct apprenticeship
text: Meat from beasts killed ahead of the cold season spoiled within days, and country households had no artificial cold to fall back on; once the store turned, hunger followed. Salt offered the first way out. Cooks noticed that a heavily concentrated brine drew the water out of the tissues, and that micro-organisms could no longer multiply in what was left. The method grew finer as aromatic berries, dried peel and bitter roots went into the bath, so that keeping the meat came to season it as well. Smoking was added on top, laying a protective film over the exposed surface. None of it was ever written down. It travelled from one valley to the next by watching and doing, an older hand showing a younger one, and it reshaped what people ate wherever regular trade never reached.

units: the difference between the two doughs lies in the microbes living in them
a starter brings together wild ferments and acidifying bacteria
the yeast sold in packets carries only one selected species
starter dough gives a crumb with uneven holes
yeast dough gives a crumb that is more even and more neutral
fermentation with a starter calls for a whole night of waiting
fermentation with yeast reaches its end far sooner
the outer crust of the starter loaf browns more deeply
the acids produced by fermentation feed the browning reactions
text: So what really sets a loaf raised on a starter apart from one raised with shop yeast? It comes down to who lives in the dough. A starter holds a whole crowd of wild ferments alongside acidifying bacteria, while the yeast sold in packets carries a single selected species and nothing more. You taste that crowd in the crumb: ragged, uneven holes, a gentle sharpness, a smell somewhere near hazelnut. Yeast crumb turns out tidier, milder, rather well behaved by comparison, with holes of much the same size all the way through. The rising splits them too. The first wants a whole night; the second is done after a short wait on the worktop. And the crust of the starter loaf goes darker, because the acids thrown off during fermentation feed the browning reactions. Patience or speed, then, and you take your pick.

units: a power cut struck a kitchen team during a banquet
the ovens stopped while poultry was only half cooked
the chilled cabinets stopped holding their temperature
the darkness forced the brigade to work by hand-held lamps
an emergency gas burner served to finish off the meats
tubs of crushed ice took over from the chilled cabinets
a section head improvised a faster form of service
the guests noticed nothing of the incident
text: A power cut caught a kitchen team halfway through a banquet, and the account they give of that evening is worth setting down. Three problems arrived at the same moment, one on top of the other. The ovens died with the poultry only half cooked. The chilled cabinets stopped holding their temperature, putting the creams and the mousses at risk. Darkness left the brigade working under hand torches propped against the shelves. The answer came from three things that lay to hand. An emergency gas burner was lit and the meats were finished off in simmering stock. Tubs of crushed ice took the place of the cabinets. A section head reworked the order of service on the spot, sending plates out one by one rather than by table. The guests, so management insists, never guessed at the scramble behind the swing door.

units: you must choose a vessel of fired clay with a stout handle
the lid has to close without leaving any gap
the aromatic bath is made up the day before
the meat is laid into that bath piece by piece
the resting happens overnight in a cool place
the liquid deepens and the flesh darkens while it waits
the meat is then seared over a fierce heat
the strained liquid serves to moisten the cooking
the covered cooking carries on beside the hearth
the meat is ready when a fork goes in without effort
text: Begin with a vessel of fired clay, one with a stout handle that will not give and a lid that settles down without the least gap. The night before, pour in the bath: a scented oil, a mild vinegar, leaves bruised between the fingers. Lay the meat down piece by piece, unhurried, the way stones are set into a low wall. Then leave the night to do its work somewhere cool and dark. In the morning, lift the lid: the liquid will have deepened, and the flesh will have taken on a duller, quieter shade. Sear it over a fierce heat, then moisten the pot with the bath you have strained. Cover it again and let it be forgotten beside the hearth through a long afternoon. Serve at last, when a fork slides in and meets nothing at all, and when the thickened sauce coats the back of a spoon with a bright film.

units: a cooperative plant records a rise in rejected products
the line in question packs soups
the cooling that follows heat treatment starts too late
the product stays in a temperature band that suits resistant spores
this exposure makes the closures bulge
a souring becomes noticeable in the product
fouling of the plate exchanger cuts down heat transfer
chemical cleaning spaced too far apart is held to blame
management plans an additional washing cycle
probes will be fitted at the entrance to the tunnel
text: Technical management at a cooperative processing plant reports a rise in rejected units on the line that packs soups. The analysis points to a single cause. Cooling after heat treatment begins with a measurable delay, so the product lingers in a temperature band where resistant spores thrive. That drawn-out exposure shows up as bulging lids and a souring that comes through in the taste. The plate exchanger stands accused: fouling has built up little by little and the transfer coefficient has fallen with it. Chemical cleaning has been spaced too far apart, and the flow of chilled water no longer makes up the loss. Managers have announced an extra washing cycle, and probes are to be fitted at the entrance to the tunnel. A check on how the vats close will round out the measures.

units: the ripening room lies in a cellar beneath a stone vault
the cheeses rest on boards of resinous wood
the level of moisture falls when the way in is left open
the surface of the cheeses hardens because of this drying
a shallow basin of water was set along a cold wall
what evaporates from that basin makes good the losses of moisture
the wooden door was replaced by a soft-closing leaf
a hanging measuring device warns the team before the critical threshold
text: The ripening room lies in the cellar of an old building, beneath a vault of grey stone. Spruce boards carry the wheels, sorted by size, and the air smells of hazelnut and damp straw. One difficulty threatens the place, all the same. As soon as the way in is left open, the moisture in the air falls away, and the rind hardens over the surface until ripening stalls beneath it. Two remedies were adopted by the people who look after the cellar. A shallow basin of water now runs along the coldest wall, and what evaporates from it makes good the losses. The old wooden door gave way to a soft-closing leaf with a low handle that can be worked with an elbow. A gauge hung from the vault warns the team before the critical threshold is crossed, and the wheels nearest the doorway are turned more often than the rest.

units: the defence of cooking at home often rests on an emotional attachment
the writer suggests comparing two meals of equivalent worth
the meal made at home costs little in raw ingredients
the amount of salt in it depends on whoever does the seasoning
this meal calls for someone to keep watch over the stove
the ready-made dish hands back a whole evening
the ready-made dish keeps without any special care
the ready-made dish imposes a fixed recipe and additives one has to accept
the decisive gap concerns control, not taste nor price
text: Standing up for cooking at home against the sealed tray tends to come from the heart, which is exactly why the argument deserves a cooler look. Set two comparable meals side by side. The first comes out of a family pan: the ingredients cost little, the salt in it depends entirely on the hand doing the seasoning, and it asks for someone to stand over the stove and watch. The second comes out of a sealed tray: it hands back a whole evening, it keeps with no special care, and it settles the recipe and the list of additives without asking the eater. Neither the flavour nor the price decides the matter in the end. What decides it is control. Cooking for yourself means keeping a say in what you swallow. That freedom is paid for in attention, and each of us can judge whether the trade is one worth making.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook reaches her workshop before the sun comes up
she grates the coloured skin of citrus straight over the dough
she keeps the candied peel in jars
her dented mould came down to her from her mother
she carries her scoring knife on her at all times
she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself
she trains one apprentice every season
she hands the baking over to her apprentices very early
she says she listens to the dough instead of imposing her will on it
text: You want to catch her pushing the workshop door open before the sun is up, apron tied high, sleeves already shoved back. The pastry cook along the road has three passions, and she will talk about every one of them without being asked twice. Citrus first: she grates the coloured skin straight over the dough so the scented oil falls where it belongs, and the candied peel goes into jars lined up on a shelf above the bench. Then old tools: the dented mould came down from her mother, the scoring knife never leaves her pocket, and she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself. Last, the apprentices. She takes one on every season, with no elaborate contract, and hands them the baking almost straight away. Ask her the secret and she shrugs: she listens to the dough rather than laying down the law to it.

units: the plain look of the room gave no hint of the quality of the meal
the first course is a clarified broth of root vegetables
this broth is striking in its depth despite being clear
the second course pairs a fish with crisp skin and a purée of bitter herbs
the cooking of the fish is judged remarkably precise
the main course disappoints because of a sauce reduced too far
the meat in that dish was nonetheless of good quality
the dessert puts the whole meal back on course
the dessert pairs an ice scented with citrus and a crisp wafer
the service is described as discreet and assured
text: Nothing in that plain room, as you push the door open, hints at how carefully the meal ahead has been built. The opening course arrives without announcement: a broth of root vegetables, clarified, clear to the bottom of the bowl, and startling in its depth. Then a piece of fish with crackling skin, set over a purée of bitter herbs; the cooking is timed to the second and deserves saying so. The central plate lets things slip, for a sauce reduced too far flattens meat of real quality and buries the aromatics under it. The dessert puts the evening back on course, a cream ice scented with sharp peel on a thin wafer that snaps under the spoon. Portions stay measured throughout, which keeps the whole thing light. The service is quiet and sure, following the rise without ever running ahead of it.
